title: Fusion exhaust processing and isotope separation
bottleneck: A fusion reactor burns only a few percent of its tritium per pass, producing a large exhaust stream of unburned deuterium-tritium mixed with helium ash that must be separated and recycled within hours. Cryogenic distillation and palladium membranes work at small scale but are slow, energy-intensive, and vulnerable to tritium inventory holdup. Faster separation directly reduces the plant's required tritium inventory. Tritium-compatible pumps, valves, and sensors must also survive years of radiation exposure without leaking, a materials challenge in its own right.
why_it_blocks: The fuel cycle's speed sets the plant's tritium inventory. Slow processing means kilograms of tritium sitting in pipes instead of burning, multiplying safety, cost, and breeding requirements.
current_state: New plasma-centrifuge approaches have demonstrated lab-scale hydrogen and lithium isotope separation. Integrated exhaust processing at reactor throughput remains unproven.
